newsitem.title: USA: GM CEO sees U.S. market share gains in 1997.
newsitem.headline: GM CEO sees U.S. market share gains in 1997.

text.p: General Motors Corp chairman and chief executive officer Jack Smith said Wednesday that he expects the automaker to aggressively increase its share of the U.S. car and truck market, following another decline during 1996.
"In 1997, we plan on aggressively increasing our U.S. share," Smith told reporters at the North American International Auto Show here.
In 1996, GM's share dipped to 31.3 percent of the U.S. car and light truck market from 32.6 percent in 1995 and 33.1 percent in 1994.
GM's total U.S. light vehicle sales fell 2.7 percent in 1996 to 4.74 million units, from 4.84 million in 1995.
Smith said the company's U.S. market share was hurt in 1996 by costly labor strikes in March and October, as well as by factory down-time to retool for new models.

But this year, he said GM is in a "strong position" with 14 new models being introduced during the 1997 model year, which will allow the company to boost its market share. In the 1960s, GM commanded half the U.S. market, and dominated as much as 45 percent of the U.S. passenger car market in the mid-1980s.
He added that GM will not sacrifice profitability to gain market share, but will stay competitive with other automakers in offering incentives.

"What we're looking for is for our products to sell themselves," Smith said. "If we're in a market where somebody else has heavy incentives, we're going to be competitive. We're going to be a player."

Worldwide, Smith said GM holds about 17 percent of the global car and truck market, and is aiming to grow that share by expanding into growth areas of the world, including Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe.
